_metadata.rubric: owner-clarified rubric with calibration anchors + no-literal-false-facts reminder, 2026-10-18
_metadata.independence: I read only u26-blind-input.json; no other file, repository search, web lookup or API was used.

hints.reason: Aragog is Hagrid's giant spider in Harry Potter (SPIDER), but he is a colony patriarch, never called a king, so KING is not reached.
King Kong gives KING as a familiar compound, but Kong is a giant ape; the cut 'spider pit' scene is trivia nobody would reach, so SPIDER is not reached.

best_available.why: At least lands SPIDER unmistakably for Potter readers and Aragog rules a spider colony, which is the nearest thing to a king on offer; still a one-sided hint.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Neither hint bridges a king and a spider; the pair needs a new route (e.g. a 'crown' or 'web' idea) rather than either of these.

hints.reason: King Arthur is instant for KING, but nothing links Arthur to SPRING (the season or any other sense).
Easter is the classic spring holiday (SPRING); KING is reached only through Christ as 'King of Kings' risen at Easter, a religious step many players will not take.
May is a spring month (SPRING); the May Day 'May King' alongside the May Queen reaches KING but is far less familiar than the Queen.

best_available.why: Reaches SPRING cleanly and has a real, if minor, King route via the May King of May Day festivities.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Both BORDERLINE hints reach spring easily and king only through a secondary tradition; the pair lacks a strong shared scene.

hints.reason: King's Cross is the famous London railway station (Harry Potter's Platform 9 3/4), giving KING via the name and TRAIN via the station, with railroad crossings as a second route to TRAIN.
Elvis is 'The King' (KING), but TRAIN is reached only via the song 'Mystery Train', which few players would summon.
Royal reaches KING directly; TRAIN depends on the British Royal Train, which is a real thing but not a scene most players picture.

best_available.why: King's Cross station is a single widely known compound that is both a king name and a train station.

pairs.pair_note: CROSS carries the pair on its own; the other two are king-first.

hints.reason: King Triton rules the sea in The Little Mermaid (KING), and Triton is a sea god living under water (WATER).
A moat is a water-filled ditch (WATER); KING is reached only via the castle the moat surrounds, one step removed.
Neptune is the Roman god and 'king of the sea' (KING), and the sea/water is his domain (WATER).

best_available.why: The Disney 'King Triton' spells out king in the character's own title and the underwater setting gives water.

pairs.pair_note: Two solid mythic/Disney routes; MOAT is a defensible castle-scene stretch but king is indirect.

hints.reason: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe has the White Witch (WITCH) and the Pevensies crowned Kings and Queens of Narnia, High King Peter among them (KING).
The three witches (WITCH) prophesy that Macbeth will be King of Scotland, which he becomes after killing King Duncan (KING).
The witches' prophecy that Macbeth shall be king covers both words, but only once the player has supplied the Macbeth frame; on its own, prophecy points at neither.

best_available.why: One play in which witches and kingship are the whole plot.

pairs.pair_note: Two excellent story routes; PROPHECY is a derivative of MACBETH and weaker.

hints.reason: The alpha wolf leads the pack (WOLF); a king is the alpha of a realm, a shared-property route like RICH for BANK+KING.
Game of Thrones is a war of kings (KING) and the Starks' direwolves and wolf sigil are its most famous animals (WOLF).
The lion is the 'king of beasts' (KING), but nothing recognizable ties a lion to WOLF beyond both being predators.

best_available.why: Game of Thrones is a single shared scene of kings and wolves.

pairs.pair_note: THRONES is the clean story route; ALPHA is a fair property route; LION is king-only.

hints.reason: 'Jedi Knight' is the standard title (KNIGHT), and Jedi wield lightsabers and follow the light side (LIGHT).
'Knight in shining armor' is a stock phrase (KNIGHT), and shining is emitting light (LIGHT).
Lightsaber gives LIGHT as a compound; a saber is a knightly sword and the Jedi Knight carries one (KNIGHT).

best_available.why: Jedi Knight plus lightsaber reaches both words through one franchise everyone knows.

pairs.pair_note: Three good hints; JEDI and SABER share the Star Wars route, SHINING is the idiom route.

hints.reason: A knight carries a shield (KNIGHT); the lion rampant is the most common beast painted on heraldic shields, e.g. England's lions (LION).
Richard the Lionheart is a crusader-knight king and the word literally contains LION, which is a rule failure.
Brave knight is a stock pairing (KNIGHT); the lion is the emblem of courage, as in the Cowardly Lion seeking it (LION), a shared-property route.
A knight's heraldic crest (KNIGHT) very commonly bears a lion (LION).

best_available.why: Courage is the property that knights and lions share in every story, and it needs no heraldry knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: LIONHEART is the best idea but a substring rule failure; the heraldry pair SHIELD/CREST are near-duplicates and both lean on knowing lions are the stock heraldic beast.

hints.reason: Armor is the knight's defining kit (KNIGHT), but nothing ties armor to MOON.
A squire kept an all-night vigil before being knighted (KNIGHT), and a vigil is kept under the moon (MOON); both sides are real but thin.
Sailor Moon reaches MOON for anime fans, but the show's heroines are 'Sailor Guardians', not knights, so KNIGHT is not reached.

best_available.why: The only hint with a foothold on both sides, via the knighting vigil kept overnight.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. 'Moon Knight' (Marvel) would be the obvious compound but it is not offered; the current set is one-sided or niche.

hints.reason: The Tale of Despereaux (book and film) is about a mouse (MOUSE) who models himself on a knight and wields a needle sword (KNIGHT); a real two-sided story, limited by name recognition.
Reepicheep is Narnia's sword-fighting talking mouse (MOUSE) made a knight of the Order of the Lion (KNIGHT), but the name is hard to recall and spell.
Knights live in castles (KNIGHT), but a mouse in a castle is not a recognizable scene players would summon from CASTLE.

best_available.why: A single character who is both mouse and would-be knight; niche but exactly on target.

pairs.pair_note: Both story hints are genuinely two-sided but niche; I gave the film-backed Despereaux the pass and held Reepicheep at borderline for recognizability. Owner may wish to pass both or neither.

hints.reason: Knights Templar reaches KNIGHT; nothing connects Templars to OCEAN.
Crusading knights give KNIGHT; sailing to the Holy Land is not how anyone pictures OCEAN.

best_available.why: Still one-sided, but at least the crusades involved sea voyages; TEMPLAR has no water at all.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Neither hint touches the ocean; the pair needs a fresh idea (e.g. 'Neptune', 'Atlantis' or 'Sir' + 'Francis Drake'-style routes).

hints.reason: Sir Francis Drake was knighted by Elizabeth I (KNIGHT) and was a privateer the Spanish called a pirate (PIRATE).
Knights fight with swords (KNIGHT) and pirates carry cutlasses and swords (PIRATE); a shared-property route.
Knight and pirate are both stock dress-up and Halloween costumes, a recognizable shared scene even if each side alone is only moderately pointed.

best_available.why: Both figures are defined by their swordplay; broad and fair.

pairs.pair_note: Three usable hints; DRAKE is the most elegant but depends on knowing Drake was knighted.

hints.reason: Lancelot is the most famous knight of the Round Table (KNIGHT) and his affair with Queen Guinevere is the core of the legend (QUEEN).
Guinevere is Arthur's queen (QUEEN), and her lover Lancelot is a knight (KNIGHT); same scene from the other side.
Knights are dubbed with a sword (KNIGHT), and it is the queen who dubs them at Buckingham Palace (QUEEN).
Knight and queen are both chess pieces, the cleanest shared category available.

best_available.why: Both targets are literally pieces on the board; nothing to explain.

pairs.pair_note: Four passes; a strong pair.

hints.reason: Knights compete in tournaments (KNIGHT); RING is reached only via boxing-tournament rings or ring-tilting, both indirect.
Jousting is the knight's sport (KNIGHT), but 'ring jousting' (spearing hanging rings) is regional trivia, so RING is not reached for most players.
The Lord of the Rings gives RING; knights swear fealty to and serve lords in the same medieval scene (KNIGHT).

best_available.why: Lord of the Rings plus the lord-and-knight feudal scene reaches both words from one familiar word.

pairs.pair_note: LORD is the only hint with a real ring; the two jousting hints never leave the tiltyard.

hints.reason: A knight is clad in metal armor (KNIGHT) and a robot is a metal man (ROBOT); the shared material is the obvious visual link between the two figures.
Armor defines the knight (KNIGHT); a robot's metal plating is routinely described as armor and an armored knight looks like a robot (ROBOT).
Knight Rider gives KNIGHT as a compound and a knight rides a horse; ROBOT is reached only by treating KITT, the talking AI car, as a robot.

best_available.why: The one property a player instantly sees in both a suit of armor and a robot.

pairs.pair_note: METAL is strong; ARMOR is a near-duplicate; RIDER is a clever title route whose robot half is debatable.

hints.reason: Excalibur is the sword of King Arthur and his knights (KNIGHT), popularly the sword pulled from the stone (ROCK).
Knights garrison castles (KNIGHT); a castle is built of stone and 'Castle Rock' is a name, but ROCK is a secondary association.
Stone is a synonym of ROCK; the Sword in the Stone is the Arthurian knightly scene (KNIGHT).

best_available.why: One legendary object joins the knight to the rock it was drawn from.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes via the Sword in the Stone; CASTLE is a fair but indirect material route.

hints.reason: Chivalry is the knightly code (KNIGHT); giving a rose is a chivalrous gesture, but ROSE is not what chivalry evokes first or clearly.
A lady's favor is the token (often a rose or ribbon) a knight wore at a tournament, which reaches both KNIGHT and ROSE only for players who know the custom.
The Wars of the Roses give ROSE as a familiar phrase, and those wars were fought by medieval knights (KNIGHT).

best_available.why: Wars of the Roses is a household name and places knights and roses in one scene.

pairs.pair_note: WARS is the only hint that lands rose clearly; the courtly-love hints need the player to know the custom.

hints.reason: 'Worth his salt' gives SALT as an idiom, but no phrase or scene connects worth to KNIGHT.
Salt (sea water, road salt) is what rusts iron (SALT), and rust is the enemy of a knight's armor (KNIGHT); a genuine shared property.

best_available.why: Salt causes rust and armor suffers it; both sides are everyday knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: RUST is a neat two-sided hint; WORTH is salt-only.

hints.reason: Batman is the Dark Knight (KNIGHT) and a vigilante who strikes from the shadows at night (SHADOW).
The Dark Knight is a familiar compound (KNIGHT), and a shadow is a patch of dark (SHADOW).
The Black Knight is a stock figure (KNIGHT); SHADOW is reached only through shadows being black, a colour association weaker than DARK's.

best_available.why: The Dark Knight who lives in the shadows; a single character covers both targets.

pairs.pair_note: BATMAN and DARK are the same route and both work; BLACK is a weaker colour variant.

hints.reason: A lance is the knight's jousting weapon (KNIGHT); nothing links a lance to SHARK.
Armor is the knight's kit (KNIGHT); shark skin denticles being 'armor' is biology trivia no player would reach.

best_available.why: Equally one-sided as LANCE, but shark-skin armor is at least a documented notion; the pair really needs a new hint such as 'fin' or 'Templar' is not it.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Both hints are knight-only; the pair needs a genuine bridging word.

hints.reason: Knights slay dragons and serpents in every legend (KNIGHT), and slaying a snake is the same verb scene (SNAKE).
St George is the dragon-slaying knight (KNIGHT); his dragon is often drawn as a great serpent, but SNAKE is a step beyond what the name evokes.
Serpent is a synonym of SNAKE; the serpent/dragon is the knight's classic foe (KNIGHT).

best_available.why: A verb route that puts knight and snake in one action.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes from the dragon-slaying scene; GEORGE is the same scene but dragon-not-snake makes it borderline.

hints.reason: Shelob is the giant spider of The Lord of the Rings (SPIDER), fought by Sam the hobbit, not by any knight, so KNIGHT is not reached.
Armor is the knight's kit (KNIGHT); nothing recognizable ties it to SPIDER.

best_available.why: Still one-sided, but a sword fight against a monstrous spider is at least a knightly scene for Tolkien readers.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Both hints sit entirely on one side.

hints.reason: May is a spring month (SPRING); no phrase or scene links May to KNIGHT.
Knights' tournaments give KNIGHT; the tradition of spring and Pentecost tournaments is not something players know, so SPRING is not reached.

best_available.why: One-sided like MAY, but Arthurian tournaments were held at spring feasts, which is marginally more of a bridge than May has to knights.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The two hints each cover a single target.

hints.reason: Star Wars gives STAR; its Jedi Knights, and knights at war generally, give KNIGHT.
Sir is the knight's title (KNIGHT); the stars who get knighted (Sir Elton John, Sir Paul McCartney) supply STAR in the celebrity sense.
Jedi Knight (KNIGHT) is a Star Wars title (STAR).

best_available.why: Jedi Knight in Star Wars reaches both words through one name.

pairs.pair_note: A strong pair; JEDI and WARS are the same franchise, SIR is an independent celebrity route.

hints.reason: A page is the first stage of knightly training (KNIGHT, TRAIN via 'training'), but the word has many stronger meanings and the knight link is weaker than SQUIRE's.
The Hogwarts Express is the famous train (TRAIN); the Knight Bus and the giant wizard-chess knight in the first film supply KNIGHT within the same world.
A squire is a knight's apprentice (KNIGHT) who trains to become one (TRAIN via ordinary inflection 'training').

best_available.why: The squire is by definition a knight in training, so both words sit in the one word.

pairs.pair_note: SQUIRE and PAGE share the training route; HOGWARTS reaches knight only via secondary Potter lore.

hints.reason: The Lady of the Lake gives Arthur's knights Excalibur and Lancelot is 'du Lac' (KNIGHT); a lake is a body of water (WATER).
A moat is the water around a castle (WATER), and the castle with its moat is the knight's home ground (KNIGHT).
The Holy Grail is the knights' quest (KNIGHT); as a drinking cup it holds water or wine, which reaches WATER only by inference.

best_available.why: Lady of the Lake is Arthurian legend's own knight-and-water scene.

pairs.pair_note: Two good passes; GRAIL is knight-first with a thin cup-to-water step.

hints.reason: Armor is knight-only; nothing connects it to WITCH.
The three witches make WITCH immediate, but Macbeth is a thane and general, not a knight, so KNIGHT is reached only by mislabelling him.
Knights go on quests (KNIGHT); quests to defeat a witch (Oz, Narnia) exist but WITCH is not what quest evokes on its own.

best_available.why: The only hint with a foothold on both sides, through the fairy-tale quest against a witch.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. MACBETH would be strong for KING+WITCH but Macbeth is not a knight; the pair needs a different story hint.

hints.reason: Wolves hunt in packs and are themselves hunted (WOLF); the hunt was the medieval knight's sport and wolf hunts a knightly scene (KNIGHT).
Game of Thrones has knights and direwolves, and wolves hunt game, but GAME alone points clearly at neither word.
The Stark wolf sigil is the most famous sigil in Game of Thrones (WOLF), and knights bear sigils (KNIGHT), but the word itself is niche vocabulary.

best_available.why: Hunting is a shared verb scene that both knight and wolf occupy.

pairs.pair_note: HUNT passes; the two Game of Thrones hints are real but rely on that one show.

hints.reason: Leo is the lion sign (LION); being ruled by the Sun is astrology trivia and does not reach LIGHT.
The Lion King and 'king of beasts' give LION; nothing links king to LIGHT.
Sunlight gives LIGHT; the lion as a sun symbol and the sunrise of The Lion King reach LION only loosely.

best_available.why: The only hint that touches both: sunlight plus the lion's sun imagery.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Two hints are lion-only; SUN is a defensible but soft stretch.

hints.reason: 'Pale moonlight' is a stock phrase: the moon is pale (MOON) and pale light is light (LIGHT).
The moon reflects sunlight; reflect is what light does and what the moon is known for.
The moon is the night's light: night light is a compound (LIGHT) and the moon belongs to the night sky (MOON).

best_available.why: States the actual relationship between the two targets.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; a natural pair.

hints.reason: A laser is a beam of light (LIGHT) and a laser mouse is a standard computer peripheral (MOUSE).
Optical means to do with light (LIGHT) and the optical mouse is the common computer mouse (MOUSE).
Night light gives LIGHT; mice are nocturnal and 'not even a mouse' stirs on Christmas night, but MOUSE is a soft reach.

best_available.why: Laser mouse is a familiar compound and a laser is light itself.

pairs.pair_note: The two computer-mouse hints are both good; NIGHT is light-first.

hints.reason: Daylight gives LIGHT and day is the opposite of NIGHT.
Contains both target words as substrings; a rule failure however apt.
Stars are points of light (LIGHT) seen in the night sky (NIGHT).
A lamp gives light (LIGHT), and lamps are lit at night, the bedside lamp being a night scene (NIGHT).

best_available.why: Lights that only appear at night.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; NIGHTLIGHT fails on the substring rule.

hints.reason: Sunset is the fading daylight (LIGHT) and the postcard sunset is over the ocean (OCEAN).
Contains LIGHT as a substring; a rule failure despite the perfect sea connection.
Bioluminescence is living light (LIGHT) best known from glowing plankton and deep-sea creatures (OCEAN); accurate but a long, hard word.
A beacon is a guiding light (LIGHT), and the classic beacon is a lighthouse warning ships at sea (OCEAN).

best_available.why: Delivers the lighthouse idea without containing the target word.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; LIGHTHOUSE is the obvious bridge but illegal, and BEACON substitutes for it.

hints.reason: Contains LIGHT; also the pirate link (ships at sea) is indirect.
A lantern is a light (LIGHT); the pirate swinging a lantern on deck or in a cave is a stock image of pirate stories and rides (PIRATE).
A flare is a burst of light (LIGHT); distress flares belong to ships generally, not pirates, so PIRATE is barely reached.

best_available.why: The one light source that belongs to the pirate's visual world.

pairs.pair_note: LANTERN is a moderate pass on the strength of the pirate-ship scene; the other two do not land pirate fairly.

hints.reason: A candle is a light (LIGHT); 'Candle in the Wind' honoured a princess, not a queen, and no other route reaches QUEEN.
Light bulb gives LIGHT; nothing connects a bulb to QUEEN.
A crown is the queen's emblem (QUEEN); nothing recognizable links crown to LIGHT.

best_available.why: Reaches queen cleanly; glittering crown jewels are the faintest nod to light, but it is still one-sided.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. All three hints are single-target; the pair needs a bridging idea (e.g. a 'Queen' band song about light, or a Lite/Dairy Queen-type brand route).

hints.reason: The selfie ring light is a familiar gadget, giving RING and LIGHT in one compound.
Sparkle is flashes of light (LIGHT) and a diamond ring sparkles (RING).
A halo is a ring of light, so it is both a RING and a LIGHT.

best_available.why: Literally a ring of light.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; a strong pair.

hints.reason: An LED is a light (LIGHT); glowing LED eyes and panels are the stock look of a robot (ROBOT).
Blinking lights give LIGHT; the beeping, blinking robot is a cliche, but blinking alone points at eyes before robots (ROBOT).
A laser is a light beam (LIGHT) and the laser-firing robot is a sci-fi staple (ROBOT).

best_available.why: The light source that visually defines a robot's face and panels.

pairs.pair_note: All three are light-first; LED and LASER reach robot through familiar imagery, BLINKING less directly.

hints.reason: Glow is light (LIGHT); glow-in-the-dark pebbles or fluorescent minerals are too niche for ROCK to be reached.
Rock concert is a stock compound (ROCK), and the light show is a defining part of a concert (LIGHT).
Lava is molten rock that cools into lava rock (ROCK); it glows and the lava lamp is a light (LIGHT).

best_available.why: Glowing molten rock plus the lava lamp reach both words from one familiar word.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; GLOW is light-only.

hints.reason: Rose-tinted glasses give ROSE; a tint is a shade of colour or coloured light, which reaches LIGHT only loosely.
Dawn is first light (LIGHT); the rosy dawn, Homer's 'rosy-fingered', reaches ROSE as a colour association rather than the flower.
Sunset is fading light (LIGHT); its pink-rose sky reaches ROSE only as a colour.

best_available.why: First light with the strongest rose-colour phrase behind it ('rosy dawn').

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. All three hints reach rose only as a colour; DAWN is the most defensible and could be promoted if the owner accepts the colour route for this pair.

hints.reason: Salt forms crystals (SALT); crystal refracts and catches light and Crystal Light is a drink brand (LIGHT).
A lamp gives light (LIGHT) and the Himalayan salt lamp is a well-known product (SALT).
Salt is sodium chloride (SALT); the yellow sodium streetlight is a familiar light source (LIGHT).

best_available.why: The salt lamp is a single everyday object that is both targets.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; a strong pair.
